headline: A safety catch I designed would have jammed the moment it was needed most. The engine lane spotted it before it shipped, and it is fixed.
matters: Reference bytes for the game were twice frozen without this repo's real test suite ever running, and a wrong number rode along unnoticed. I am building the enforcement so that cannot happen quietly again. My first design had a trap: if a freeze failed its tests for a reason that needed a second freeze to fix, the first one could never be signed off - and the only ways out were to hand-edit the record or to sign off something that had not passed. Those are precisely the two things the catch exists to prevent, so it would have taught people to do the wrong thing at the exact moment it mattered. The fix lets a failed freeze be formally set aside instead, but only by actually doing the replacement, so it cannot become a shortcut. Separately, the engine lane answered the question I could not: the signature has to record how many of the strict checks actually ran, because that is the one number a suite run WITHOUT the strict flag cannot produce - and a suite without the flag is otherwise fully green and indistinguishable.

headline: Four numbers describing the cartridge's own size had quietly gone wrong, and the one that fooled the search was the one that looked most correct.
matters: These are the figures that say how long each build of the game is. Nothing in the project read them any more, so nothing could notice when they drifted - one was right the day it was typed and wrong within a month, and it stayed wrong for 28 days. The search that found them was looking for numbers typed in by hand, so it missed a fourth that was written as a NAME instead of a number: it looked like the computer had worked it out, and it hadn't - it was the wrong build's figure. The fix removes the stored numbers entirely, so the game works them out fresh every time and there is nothing left to go stale. There is now a check that would have caught all four.

headline: We now know how much of the game's code the timing model can actually speak about - and measuring it turned up two ways the model can hand back a confident wrong number.
matters: The emulator lane was waiting on this figure. The answer depends entirely on how you count, so it is reported two ways rather than one, and the gap between them is itself the finding. More useful than the headline number: of the game's routines, about one in six could carry a timing budget and exactly one does. The two defects are the kind worth having found early - the timing built-in never checks which of the console's two processors it is on, so on the main chip it can hand back a figure measured in the other chip's clock units; and the sound-side adder tops out instead of refusing, returning its ceiling as though it were an answer. Neither can be reached by today's code, both by luck rather than design. Nothing is fixed yet; they are written down with the conditions that would close them.

Four brief corrections upheld: model is four-valued not three (Branch pairs); 'cannot time' is two different things (five unreachable trap #0 vs a deliberate Z80 demand subset); shipped_shapes() misses the seam-1 resident sound blob entirely (registry walk sees zero Z80 in every sound-on shape); Layer A/B is the axis, not the denominator. headline: The check that was supposed to catch tests quietly opting out could never have failed - it was reading output the test runner throws away.
matters: Before a batch of the game's reference bytes is accepted, this repo runs its tests and requires that none of them quietly opted out. That requirement has been part of the ritual for a long time and it has never once been able to fail: the test runner hides the output of any test that passes, so the warning line it was looking for was always discarded before anyone could grep for it. Every landing that reported 'none opted out' - including two of mine tonight - was reporting on an empty page. It took one word on the command line to fix. The automated nightly check already had that word and was never blind, so the damage is bounded to hand-run landings. Separately, 30 tests across 11 files worded their opt-out in ways the check could not match even with the output visible; those now share one spelling, defined in one place, with a lint that fails if a new one drifts.

headline: A landing gate I wrote would have taken the nightly safety net dark on its first night, by tripping the exact alarm it was built to restore.
matters: The new lint prints a one-line summary saying all the opt-out warnings are correctly worded - and that summary quoted the warning text itself. The nightly check greps the log for that text and shuts the whole lane down when it finds it, on the assumption that a test went quiet. So a perfectly healthy run of the new gate would have looked exactly like the failure it exists to detect, every night, starting the first. It only surfaced because I had just fixed the blindness above; with the old command the line was invisible and it would have shipped. The gate now describes the warning instead of printing it, and refuses to run if its own summary ever contains it again.

headline: Reference bytes for the game can no longer be accepted on top of a batch whose tests were never actually run - the tool now runs them itself.
matters: Twice recently a batch of reference bytes was frozen without this repo's real tests ever running, because the written recipe was missing one setting that turns the strict checks on. Nobody audits a command line for a missing setting, so the recipe looked complete and was inert. The fix stops relying on anyone remembering it: the tool runs the suite itself, sets that switch itself, and records what it found. The record contains one number that a run WITHOUT the switch physically cannot produce, so a signed-off batch cannot be a batch that was never properly tested. If a batch genuinely fails its tests and the fix needs a fresh batch, the old one can be formally set aside - but only by someone who actually ran the tests and got a red result, so setting-aside cannot become the easy way out.

headline: Both ways the timing checker could hand back a confident wrong number are closed - one of them so that the mistake can no longer be written down at all.
matters: The game has two processors. The tool that measures how long a stretch of code takes only knows how to time the sound chip, but never checked which processor it was on - so on the main chip it could return a figure measured in the wrong chip's clock, and one padding instruction is spelled the same on both, so the wrong number would have looked right. It now refuses, and the refusal explains which chip you are on, why the number would be wrong, and the two correct ways to ask. I had suggested it fall back to the main chip's own timing table; the agent showed that would be worse - that table often gives an upper bound rather than an exact figure, and this tool's answers get compared for equality, so it would assert a cost the machine need not pay. The second: the sound-side adder used to stop at its ceiling and return the ceiling as an answer. It now cannot overflow at all - the limit is derived and checked when the compiler builds, so narrowing it is a build failure rather than a silent return of a wrong number. I reproduced that proof myself.
detail: Landed fc3dee76 (2a72ba48, bad9390a, cb29b2a3). CYCLES-CPU-GUARD: ruled REFUSE not dispatch; require_z80_for_timing raises [cycles.wrong-cpu] on Cpu::M68000 and on absent ev.cpu. Agent's deciding reason overturned my brief: ~1/3 of the shipped 68000 stream prices Fixed{exact:false} (a ceiling, mostly because operand width is a linker-relaxation fact the evaluator precedes), and cycles() is compared with ==, so summing ceilings into an equality asserts a cost the machine need not have - i.e. defect 2's shape in a new place. Also pad_to_cycles cannot dispatch (its pad units are Z80 nop/jr; jr has no 68000 spelling) and units differ (3.58MHz T-states vs 7.67MHz). Old [cycles.unknown-op] 'add it to z80_cycles' text now reachable only from a Z80 proc where it is correct. SPAN-COST-WIDTH: TStates=u128, MAX_SPAN_T_STATES derived in-type from Cost::Fixed's u16 payload x (isize::MAX/size_of::<CodeItem>()), plus const _: () = assert!(<= i128::MAX) proving the lossless reach to Value::Int; const overflow is a BUILD error so the width is compiler-checked, not runtime-watched. Reproduced by me: narrowing to u64 gives error[E0080] 'attempt to compute 64051194700380387_u64 * 65535_u64, which would overflow', restore exit 0. The ledger's own suggested u32/u64+bail fallback misses the derived bound by ~230x. 8 gates, all red-first; ONE poison came back green and it was the matcher not the guard (asserted the refusal doesn't name z80_cycles, but the new refusal legitimately names it as the table it reads) - retightened to the real property, re-proved red. Brief corrections: two pad_to_cycles sites not one; the dense case does emit but is rejected downstream by the 68000 mnemonic table (diagnostic-quality, not miscompilation) while cycles() and SPARSE pad_to_cycles built completely clean with no diagnostic - worse than the case I flagged. headline: The crash-screen guard could report success by having nothing to check. It now proves, per build shape, that it had something.
matters: When the game crashes, a debug build prints a report naming where it happened. That report only works if a particular block of vendored code is the very last thing in the cartridge, and a check guards it. The check had a hole: if the block went missing entirely - renamed, or dropped by a re-layout - it returned success, because it looked for the block, did not find it, and treated that as nothing to complain about. A missing subject and a satisfied rule produced the same answer. It now works out, for each of the seven ways we build the cartridge, whether that build is supposed to carry the block at all, and complains in both directions: a build that should have it and does not, and a build that should not and does. Six of the seven carry it. The check also refuses if either group is empty, because a rule that applies to nothing passes trivially.

headline: Numbers written in comments cannot be wrong, because nothing runs them. Fifty-nine of ours were, and five were teaching people not to look.
matters: A comment saying a piece of the game is a certain size is read by people and executed by nothing, so it can be wrong for months without anything going red. Five of ours went further: they claimed a region was the SAME size in both the normal and the debug build, when the generated table says the two differ. A wrong number misinforms you; a wrong claim that two things match tells you there is nothing to check. Several files disagreed with themselves inside one screen. The fix is not to write in the right number - that is the same mistake with a fresher date - but to point at where the number actually lives, so it cannot drift again.
detail: PROSE-SWEEP, merged in 537869e6 (branch sweep/prose-bounds, commits 49666597 + b60e79cb + notes 248b18f5/3d8c9d64). 8 false-or-stale '$X both shapes' length claims; 51 stale reference windows across 15 port gates, of which ZERO matched a current pins.rs region. Two enumeration parameters run and reconciled (numeric-literal-in-comment A1-A4: 1348/1432/4661/1309; bound-language keyword K1-K5: 276/107/30/14), queries listed verbatim and re-runnable in docs/superpowers/notes/2026-08-27-prose-bounds-sweep.md, because an empty sweep and a grep that never matched its subject are the same artifact. Joint commitment with the aeon lane, each lane over its own tree. Patterns that transfer: the half-fix (a pointer added, the copy left beside it) is the dominant mode; the invariance claim rots before the number does; derived diagnostics that interpolate {max} are immune to the class. Explicitly NOT covered: decimal-only bounds (A3's 4661 hits untriaged), .emp/.asm, and empyrean's SIGIL_* specs - a real gap, unswept by either lane. repin.toml BLOCKED (other lane's file) and its per-region comments carry the identical stale claims, so the generator's INPUT is stale too.

headline: Our freeze tool wrote a record file it could not read back, noticed, and left it there. It corrupted one tonight.
matters: Every time the two projects are frozen together, a line is added to a record file saying which build is which. That line includes a sentence a human wrote. If the sentence contained a quotation mark - and sentences quote things - the tool wrote a file that was no longer readable, checked it, found it broken, and left the broken file in place. Nothing about it looks broken: it looks authoritative, and every later check fails with a line number instead of a cause. It is now checked before it is written, quotes are handled properly rather than refused, and the file is replaced in a way that cannot leave it half-written.
detail: FREEZE-WRITES-HOME ledger half. Merged in 537869e6 (branch fix/provenance-ledger-integrity, f386109c). Root cause: render_entry hand-built TOML basic strings while toml_str - the correct escaper - sat directly beneath it, serving the other two renderers; its doc comment asserted its fields 'never carried a quote', and that sentence WAS the defect (the same prose class as the sweep above, in the function it broke). Now: every field through toml_str; fault_in_prose refuses only what a one-line field cannot show verbatim (control chars incl. raw newline) naming character and byte offset; fault_in_key guards the table-header interpolation which has no escaping fallback; append_block parses in memory BEFORE installing; write_atomic temp+sync_all+rename, both bare fs::write sites gone (grep on the committed blob returns 0). Gate is the CLASS not the instance - 'after any refreeze that reports an error, provenance.toml still parses' - proven red-first reproducing tonight's exact 'expected newline, #' at line 16 col 9, plus the_refusal_accepts_every_entry_the_chain_already_holds as a control so an over-strict refusal could not land quietly. RECORDED: temp-and-rename would NOT have prevented this - an atomic rename installs a complete-but-invalid file atomically - and that conflation was the fix both lanes had agreed on this morning. TAGGED, still open: no end-to-end refreeze --freeze has run through the assembled CLI path.

headline: The assembler can now say whether the edits in its tree actually reach the program, instead of warning about every stray note.
matters: The assembler prints whether its own source tree has uncommitted changes. It could not tell an edit to real code from a note left in a documentation folder, so it warned constantly and was therefore read by nobody. It now works out which files the program is genuinely built from and reports against those. The engine lane reads this line, and their reader used to treat any word it did not recognise as safe - so a new word would have silently switched their check off. They fixed that first; ours landed second.
detail: VERSION-DIRT-CLASSIFY. Merged in 537869e6 (branch feat/version-drift-classify, 8c1dce0f + 9d71d8f4, held ~5h at the aeon lane's request and landed only after their guard fix aeon 4b43bdda and their attest at sigil 866ab37a). build.rs derives the compiled-source closure from cargo metadata --no-deps (transitive non-dev path-dep walk, every closure manifest a rerun trigger, no hand-written crate list); banner gains closure:, closure-revision:, closure-paths:; tree: reports clean-sources when uncommitted changes fall outside the closure. Four gates, each proven red by mutation: reported paths equal cargo's answer re-derived at test time; reported revision is the last commit touching those paths (proven under a docs-only tip, the only tree state where they differ); no compiled source reaches a file the closure calls unreachable via #[path]/include*!; the banner discloses which way it errs. False-clean gated in both places. NOTE, measured 2026-08-27 and it kills a hoped-for remedy: narrowing the paired-landing banner to the closure does NOT silence it - pins.rs is a non-dev path dep of sigil-cli, pub mod pins carries no cfg(test), and native.rs (the module the CLI calls at build time) reads pins values - so that banner is a TRUE positive every time it fires.

headline: The freeze tool now writes into the copy of the repo you run it from, not the one it was built from - and it says out loud when those differ.
matters: Freezing the two projects together is done from a private working copy so the shared one is left alone. That protection did not work: the tool wrote into whichever copy it had been BUILT from, so a freeze meant to stay private silently modified ten files in a colleague's working copy. It now writes where it is run, refuses by name if it cannot tell where that is, and prints on every run which copy it was built from versus which it is operating on - because the underlying trap is that a pre-built program carries its old paths, options and defaults silently, and a stale one answers confidently about all of them.
detail: FREEZE-WRITES-HOME, both halves, merged 38fa6096 (branches fix/harness-root-derived 5335f01e + fix/repin-root-passed 0aada5a2). Half one: HARNESS_ROOT demoted to a display-only BUILT_FROM; root derived via git rev-parse --show-toplevel of the cwd + crates/sigil-harness, verified against BOTH markers (golden/provenance.toml and repin.toml), refusing by name with resolved/from-where/expected-and-missing; SIGIL_HARNESS_ROOT override verified identically, set-but-empty refused; NO fallback to the constant, held by a source lint that was mutation-checked. Half two was NOT optional: refreeze shells repin via cargo run, and cargo REUSES an artifact across trees sharing one CARGO_TARGET_DIR - measured here on the real crate, build-from-B finished in 0.01s still baking tree A's path - so half one alone would have written goldens to one tree and pins.rs to another, a split freeze from a tool reporting success. repin now takes --harness-root and refreeze passes it on both spawn paths incl. REPIN_BIN; disagreeing flag-vs-env is refused naming BOTH rather than ranked. Six red-first reversals, each restored; headline gate spawns the real binary with the real argument list from a third valid tree and asserts non-vacuity first. announce_root prints unasked on every invocation and states the verdict in words when the paths differ - specified that way at the aeon lane's insistence, against their own convenience, because a diagnostic behind a flag only reaches people who already suspect the binary.

headline: Two of my test expectations broke on the engine lane's parcel; one is now written so it can only fail for its own reasons.
matters: Their change to how slopes are judged shifted things by two bytes, and two of my checks went red. Neither was their fault. One was a test compiling a single file with a narrower notion of where the project starts than the real build uses, so a file path that works in the real build missed in the test. The other is a deliberate tripwire holding a hand-typed address, designed to force a human to notice and explain movement. Rather than typing in the new number I anchored it to a generated one plus an offset, so a shift somewhere else in the program can no longer set it off, while a change in the part it actually watches still does.
detail: SLOPE-HARNESS-FIX, f7266c65. Cause 2: test_p2_player_states_port lowered with include_root narrowed to games/sonic4/player and embed_base None, so the parcel's new root-relative embed("engine/data/sine.bin") joined onto the module dir; both fields moved to the aeon root, matching main.rs and soundbankhead_port.rs. Cause 1: Ground_Move_Cap derived from the build (plain 0x10914, debug 0x10A24) not transcribed, then written as pins::P_STATE_GROUND.plain/.debug + 0x2F4 - the intra-region offset grew 0x2F2 to 0x2F4 in BOTH shapes, which says the +2 landed INSIDE the region ahead of the symbol rather than sliding the region whole, a sharper statement than the +2-both-shapes I was given. PROCESS DEFECT, mine: I first named test_p1_player_port to the aeon lane, having grepped for the SHAPE of the cause and stopped at the first match instead of tracing from the failing-test names I already held; caught only because their uncommitted red-attest record listed the six by name. The artifact kept for honesty was load-bearing for correctness inside the hour. I also described the fix as one line when it needs both fields, the exact separation they had corrected me on an hour earlier.

headline: The file-embedding word in our language works from the project root - except for one file, which is exempted by name in a line of my tool.
matters: When engine source embeds a data file, the path is read from the project root. One file writes its path relative to itself instead, and it works only because a single line names that file specifically. So a new file copying that style silently fails, and the style it copies is not a feature - it is an exception. I could not answer this by reading for most of the day; it took a trace plus deliberately breaking the exception to prove the line was doing the work rather than just sitting there.
detail: EMBED-BASE-RULE, note landed 6943cde3. Mechanism is native.rs::build_emp's embed_base_for closure: `if id == "engine.math" { math_dir } else { aeon_root }` - a third closure I had missed after finding two module-independent ones. Proven by trace to resolve_sandbox_path with observed values at the containment check, corroborated by the traced build being byte-identical to the frozen s4.bin (34c67ea6/718999) so it IS the ROM path, and by counterfactual: gating the arm off reproduces the two predicted [sandbox.path-escape] errors. Two prior hypotheses refuted first (a try-root-then-fallback resolver; math.emp being dead code). Further: only `data` items thread embed_base - const/equ/offsets/table/dispatch take include_root alone; and the base is the CONSUMING evaluation's, not the defining module's, so one spelling is legal in one item and refused from another. Proposal to the owner (language surface, so his call): respell math.emp's two sites root-relative and delete the exception, byte-neutral, making the rule uniform and stateable. Caveats kept from the agent: only canonical plain was actually built, and the rule is asserted for embed() not import().

headline: Checked which layout rules the build already enforces before asking anyone to enforce them again - three did, and one nobody had written down does not.
matters: We were about to hand the engine lane eight layout rules to police. Three of them the build already refuses to proceed on, so handing those over would have built a second guard for a rule that already stops the build - work for nothing, and a second place to keep in step. Two are genuinely unguarded, and one of those is new: a deliberately empty gap in the cartridge has nothing checking that it stays empty. That was proven by filling it and watching the build accept it, then proving the same check DOES fire on a different violation - so the pass is the check declining to look, not a broken test.
detail: EIGHT-CONSTRAINTS-RECHECK, merged 61826768 (branch audit/constraint-recheck, 136332d4). already-asserted+demonstrated: R1a (validate_placement [map.undeclared-island]/[map.anchor-absent]), R3 (relax::bank_diag), R8 (check_error_handler_is_last - all three of the inventory's outstanding asks landed in-tree since at 1a03c75c/83b6610e/2247b0f2). NOT asserted: R1b, R1c, R1d, R6 (negative; only a warning in a binary no ROM build runs), R9 (negative, NEW, no inventory row). R9 demonstrated absent with a positive control on the same loop. R3's coverage is narrower than the inventory records: bank_diag skips any section without a bank: declaration (verified firsthand) and .emp makes bank:/vma: mutually exclusive, so soundbankhead is vma:-phased and outside it and dac_banks has no section declaration - both bank heads the anchors name are unchecked and rest on R1c, which nothing asserts. Two inventory premises rotted: map bases are no longer cosmetic, and seam2::bank_anchors_from_str now keys anchors BY NAME on the shipped path, giving up the invariant the ledger comment rests on. Seven predicates delivered in aeon's five-field shape, value as derivation not number. R2/R4 unclassifiable and said so. NOT a closed set: aeon's build-side gates unenumerated, check_object_bank_budget unclassified, off-canonical shapes not individually checked. Also flagged to aeon, not touched: dac_banks.emp's header still says $48000/$50000, superseded by the re-layout to 0x90000/0x98000.

headline: Wrote the check for the reserved gap, and it immediately found that the gap's own declaration has been wrong by six bytes since August.
matters: The cartridge reserves an empty span for a small piece of sound code, and the engine's settings file declares where that span ends. Nothing had ever checked the declaration against reality. The new check found that real content sits six bytes inside the declared gap - and my own existing test already pinned the true addresses, so the cartridge has been right and the declaration wrong the whole time. I did NOT switch the check on: three of the seven ways we build would go red, and the fault is the declaration, not the layout. Bending a new check to accommodate a wrong declaration would defeat the reason for writing it.
detail: HOLE-INTERIOR-UNGUARDED, merged 6775b449 (branch fix/hole-interior-reserved, a0d8dcd9). native::hole_interior_faults: hole opens at `after`, runs to `at`, filled_by's module is the permitted occupant DERIVED from the shape's registry; every other byte-emitting overlap is [map.hole-interior-occupied] naming hole, intruder, head label and occupied sub-span. Five distinct refusals for the unmeasurable arms (anchor-unresolved/ambiguous, bounds-degenerate, filler-unknown/absent) so the vacuous case announces itself - rebuilding the declining-to-look defect one layer up was the live risk. Both maps declare at=0x3FE; boot_data_port pins rom[0x3d0]==0xAF, idle nonzero 0x3d0..0x3f8, rom[0x3f8]==0x9F, so the idle is 0x3D0..0x3F8 and boot_tail's PSG byte sits 6 bytes inside the declared interior; the comment's $3d8 start is wrong too. Declared at aeon a7375682 2026-08-01, untouched while boot grew +8 and the idle body went 38->40. Positive control: correcting only `at` returns clean for all three affected shapes. Sound-on shapes report says-nothing not pass (when=sound_off). NOT wired into validate_placement - deliberately. Suite 4068/0/4 vs 4058/0/4, failing sets empty both, +10 exactly the new tests; all seven shipped shapes byte-identical. [map.hole-anchor-missing] pinned - it had no test anywhere and had never been observed to fire.

headline: An error the compiler threw away could put a WRONG BYTE in the cartridge while reporting nothing wrong at all.
matters: When the compiler works out a constant's value ahead of time, it did a quick trial evaluation first - and if that trial failed, it threw the error away and treated the failure as if the constant simply had no fixed value. Those are not the same thing. The consequence turned out to be worse than a missing number: the constant silently took a DIFFERENT file's value instead of its own, so a build could emit 400 where 4 was correct and report no errors. Not a value that looks obviously wrong - a value that looks plausible. The trial failure now reaches the person building, while the ordinary case of a constant that genuinely has no fixed value stays quiet.
detail: CONST-EMBED-SWALLOWED, merged 659371e3 (branch fix/const-fold-diagnostics, 85950508). fold_const_literal returned Option<i64> and dropped its diagnostics; None already meant ordinary-non-literal, so a FAILED eval was indistinguishable from one with nothing to fold. Root mechanism, found by the agent and not previously known: the probe calls eval_const_with_root WITHOUT embed_base, so it resolves embed() against include_root while real lowering resolves against the module's asset dir - probe raises [embed.not-found], error discarded, no fold, and the CONSUMER's SCALE answers instead of the definer's. Gate vs unmodified master: errors=[], image=[1,144], 400 where 4 is right. Now a three-way ConstFold; the quiet arm is corpus-derived (probe instrumented over all seven shipped shapes: 182 Error occurrences, 36 distinct, 100% unknown-name/unknown-function, zero other classes) and fails loud - rewording either message surfaces them. Faults drain through the existing seen_across_modules filter so a re-raised fault reports once. One caller, fully enumerated (ConstFoldCache::folded -> collect_pub_comptime -> ambient_items/ambient_from_uses, 4 driver sites). Byte-neutral: an errored eval still never folds; seven shapes CRC-identical AND golden/anchor gates green both sides, so matched to frozen provenance not merely to each other. Suite 4074/0/4 vs 4068/0/4, failing sets empty, +6 exactly, zero skip lines. NOT fixed and booked: the embed_base skew itself (fixing changes what folds = moves bytes). Enumeration with positive control found two other discard sites left unfixed: eval/guards.rs interp_one_part/interp_one (message degraded, error still raised) and emp_census.rs (tooling, but it is read as the authoritative clobber-undeclared list, so a truncated parse understates it).

headline: A failure whose fix changed no bytes could never be marked superseded - so a finished, tested check sat unusable behind it.
matters: Every paired freeze appends a line to a record file, and a failed run stays recorded as failed until a later freeze replaces it. But a freeze only appends when the output actually changes - so when a failure's cause turned out to be in the test harness rather than the game, fixing it produced identical output, appended nothing, and the failure stayed the newest entry indefinitely. That went from cosmetic to blocking today: a new safety check was finished and tested and could not be switched on until the record moved. An explicit request to supersede now appends even when nothing moved; without that request, nothing changes.
detail: FIXPOINT-CANNOT-SUPERSEDE, merged ce0b610b (branch feat/supersede-passes-fixpoint, 61251ef6), pushed 8dc62906. The bail was `if equals_tip { FIXPOINT; return }` with supersede consulted nowhere; now `byte_neutral && supersede.is_none()`, falling through to the UNCHANGED append gate (green tip, unattested-on-armed-chain and unarmed chain all still refused). provenance.rs +249/-0, purely additive: plan_freeze as a pure decision, freeze_into owning the ledger half. One ordinary [[entry]], no schema; legibility from the entry's own note. All seven provenance:: consumers outside refreeze verified to read tip_target only, so duplicate goldens are invisible to them. Anti-evasion intact: abandoning the new tip still costs a real red attest. Six red-first mutations, each failure shown and restored, including the two refusal sub-cases proven separately. Suite 4074/0/4 vs 4068/0/4, failing sets empty, +6 exactly. REVERSAL, logged as such: refused this morning on 'one instance is not enough to redesign a ledger on', which was right on that evidence; changed on n=2 plus a blocked consumer. NOT red-first: the early-refusal improvement at the pre-rebuild gate, gated by reasoning only - flagged rather than absorbed.

headline: The engine lane's freeze finished, my hold came off, and the ledger it wrote is one step short of finished in a way that would have stopped their next one.
matters: Their record of the run says the check came back failing. It does not say that - it says nothing at all, because the run never got written down. That is a much easier fix (just run it again, and it should pass now), but it also means the very next change that moves bytes would have been refused at the gate with no obvious reason why. Told them before they hit it.

headline: A fixture the engine lane renamed broke three of my checks, and the obvious repair would have quietly broken them worse.
matters: Their rename was correct and my check was correct; the gap was that nothing reads these references unless a build runs, and builds only run when a change moves bytes. So it surfaced two parcels later inside someone else's work, looking like their fault. The tempting fix - point at the renamed file - would have aimed three checks at a completely different rule while their names and comments still described the old one. Picked a different fixture on three stated grounds and added a check that costs no build, so the next one gets named the morning after instead.

Rejected poison_four_bands (P2a DELETED the one-band rule the old fragment pinned - a rename that is also a re-aim); rejected poison_band_orphan_restore/span_mismatch/h2_sh (COUNT 2, would redden the two [Error]==1 assertions); rejected poison_band_no_owner ('carries no band id' appears in 3 poisons + the guard, so the matcher cannot witness which rule fired). Verified in isolated worktree + own CARGO_TARGET_DIR against detached aeon b42141bc (entry 177 aeon_rev); 8/8 SIGIL_STRICT_GATE=1. Main checkout untouched, target/release/sigil still 85ba502f, no relink announcement owed. Class fix noted for the nightly source-gate lane. Also: I was reading a ledger one chain stale for the whole exchange because aeon had three commits local - undetectable from my side.

headline: The engine lane was one minute from rebuilding our shared tool out of a stale copy of my tree, and the result would have looked perfectly healthy.
matters: They told me they were about to rebuild the shared assembler and quoted the version they expected it to pick up. They had the right version in mind but were pointing at the wrong thing: the rebuild compiles whatever is sitting in my working folder, and mine was two commits behind - two commits that were their own freshly-finished work. Had they started, the tool would have been stamped with the older version while every check agreed with itself, because the check that looks closest at this compares the tool against the folder it was built from, and both would have been equally stale. I pulled the two commits first, so it built the right thing. Out of that came a rule I have now written down: when the shared tools are rebuilt, the announcement lists a fingerprint for EVERY tool the build produces, generated by a command rather than typed. My own file had a hand-written list of three, and the one it left out was the only one that actually feeds their cartridge build.
detail: Relink of target/release/sigil requested by aeon at ~02:40Z. Their message cited my origin/master b73bf420 as the reference; my main checkout was at 4eca7d93, 2 behind (b23cba42 refreeze chain 178 + b73bf420 attest, both landed through their lane). `git merge --ff-only b73bf420`, pure ff, empty b73bf420..4eca7d93, verified against `git ls-remote origin refs/heads/master` not the tracking ref. Relink completed 02:49Z: sigil md5 85ba502f->495986ee, baked rev 914846bf->b73bf420, confirmed here firsthand. RULING (mine, sigil-internal gate design, d-2 'just do it' territory): announcement emits md5 for every executable cargo build --release produces, via `find target/release -maxdepth 1 -type f -executable -printf '%p\n' | sort | xargs md5sum` - command verified to run as written, 12 lines today. Rejected aeon's proposal to name two binaries: the existing hand-list named sigil/refreeze/repin and omitted emit_sound_blob, which writes z80_sound_blob.bin, declares its output byte-deterministic from sources AND toolchain version in its own header, and is invoked by aeon build.sh as an ARTIFACT step that dies without it. n=2: aeon build.sh's ASSEMBLER PROVENANCE banner already recorded sigil sitting three days behind unnoticed. Landed in docs/OVERSEER.md under GUARD THE ARTIFACT.

headline: Their freeze was sound but its written description of what moved was wrong, and that description is what the next session will read.
matters: They asked me to check their arithmetic rather than take it, which was the right instinct. The record says the addresses shifted uniformly with one oddity; measuring all 134 of them says there are three distinct groups and two oddities, not one. The part worth their attention is that the shielding fix's 16 bytes show up in the release build's address field and never in the debug build's - which may be entirely intended, but nobody had noticed it either way. Nothing about the cartridge or the tests is wrong; only the sentence describing it, which is already committed and pushed, and which is exactly the kind of claim nothing in a repository ever checks.
detail: Chain 179 (13a6d3c8 refreeze tilt-and-instashield, 520d07f6 attest, aeon 4ba7cb92). Their commit message: 'Pins move +0x80 plain / +0x70 debug ... PLAYER_SNAP_TO_SURFACE moves +0x72 in both shapes'. Measured over all 134 changed entries (45 Region + 89 Pin) by two methods sharing no code - diff parse, and differencing named symbols read from pins.rs at both revisions. Actual: three tiers. +0x70 BOTH shapes on 21 entries (13 P_STATE_* pins, 6 PLAYER_* regions, 2 u32) plus PLAYER_COMMON whose base is unmoved while its length grows +0x70 both shapes (the tilt). +0x72 both shapes on TWO entries - PLAYER_SET_STATE as well as PLAYER_SNAP_TO_SURFACE. +0x80 plain / +0x70 debug on the remaining 112. Max debug delta anywhere in the field is 0x72; max plain is 0x80, so the insta-shield's 0x10 never enters the debug pin field though s4.debug still grew +156 total like plain. Mechanism deliberately NOT asserted to them - flagged as their measurement. Also: their message said shield=14 B, their commit says 16 B; 0x10 says the commit. Suggested repair is a correcting note in the next chain entry, not a history rewrite.

headline: The open question in my last note is answered, and the answer is that my instrument could not see what I asked it about.
matters: I reported that the shielding fix's bytes appeared in the release build's address list and never the debug one, and asked whether that was intended. They measured it three ways and the bytes are in the debug build - a tool that decodes the debug cartridge's own contents runs the new code nearly seven thousand times. What I was reading is a list of landmark addresses, and there is enough spare room between that code and the next landmark in the debug build to swallow the growth before it reaches one. So the list showed nothing while the cartridge had changed. I had scoped the claim to the list and asked rather than asserted, which is the only reason it cost a measurement instead of a wrong entry in the record. headline: The prediction we wrote down in advance came true, and their run found two real defects in my own tooling.
matters: Before they measured, both lanes committed in writing that their change would alter values without shifting anything, so no addresses should move - and that if one moved we would stop and talk rather than quietly re-record it. It held, and I checked that myself from the committed change rather than taking their word. Recording it as a promise kept rather than just a green run, because a prediction that comes true is only worth something if it is on record that it was made first. Two defects in my tools fell out of them using them: the tool that rewrites our reference cartridges cannot be aimed at a chosen copy of the tree by a flag while its safer sibling can - point it wrong and it quietly works on the wrong tree instead of failing - and it runs longer than an agent can hold a command open, so being killed leaves half-rewritten reference files behind. Both are now on the list. They also found a better way to prove one of these builds actually ran, using a file of mine neither of us had thought to read that way.

headline: I quietly worked around a wrong reference instead of saying it was wrong, and the other lane had to raise it against themselves for anyone to learn.

headline: The freeze record can now tell you when it points at a revision that no longer exists - and it found one.
matters: Every freeze pins itself to a revision of each repo, so a record cannot quietly belong to a different version of the code than it claims. Nothing ever checked those revisions still EXIST - only that they were the right length, so a revision that had been rewritten away passed forever and silently. Chain 181's record points at exactly such a ghost, created when the engine lane rewrote history between measuring and publishing. The check now reads the real remote, names the entry and the revision, and tells apart three situations that look identical but need opposite responses: you forgot to fetch, you have not pushed yet, and the revision is gone for good. The last one is the only real fault, and it is the one nothing could see.

headline: The compiler now states where each piece of the game must sit, instead of working it out from where it happens to sit.
matters: Until now, how strictly a chunk of the game had to be positioned was never written down anywhere - it was worked backwards from a frozen table of addresses. So re-freezing that table could silently change a requirement with no positioning code changing, which has already happened once and quietly broke hand-built padding elsewhere. Writing the requirements down revealed three that the old scheme could not even express: two sound sections that must start on a 32 KB boundary and the object code that needs a 64 KB one. All three were being held true only by hand-placed anchors, with the actual requirement recorded nowhere. This is the first of the rules that has to exist before those frozen tables can stop being the authority, which is what ends the freeze-per-byte ritual you asked about.

That is stable only while a frozen table holds the neighbour still, which is exactly what we are retiring. The number I briefed was 79, taken from a warning the previous pass had used as its progress meter. That warning compares addresses, and when a neighbour's label sits flush against a region's last byte an address cannot tell that apart from a label the region owns - so the meter would have read zero with 58 more cases of the same fault live underneath it. The real population is 140. Thirty-four were converted outright with nothing changing; the rest now declare what kind of contract they have, and an undeclared one refuses instead of passing quietly.

headline: The rule I broke tonight is now a command that refuses instead of a note that asks.

detail: Merged dc9cc24a: scripts/landing-run.sh. headline: I now know which of my own tests lie when the engine's source tree is missing, and which just go quiet.
matters: When the engine tree is absent or half-there, some of my tests blame the wrong thing entirely and most simply vanish from the count without failing. I measured nine different ways of it being missing, because deleting it outright turns out to find almost nothing - it is the half-broken cases that expose the lying tests. One real defect fell out: the suite creates a folder inside the very tree it is checking for, which switches other tests' safety guards off partway through a run, so the same command gives a different answer the second time you run it.
